name: Acetyl octapeptide-3
route: Applied to the skin in serums, creams and microneedle patches
status: Cosmetic ingredient; not an FDA-approved drug
mechanism: An eight-amino-acid extension of acetyl hexapeptide-8 that is meant to imitate a nerve protein and, in theory, soften signals that tighten facial muscles

article.summary: Acetyl octapeptide-3 (SNAP-8) is a skincare peptide marketed as a gentler alternative to Botox for expression lines. Published human data are limited to combination products.
article.takeaway: Acetyl octapeptide-3, nicknamed SNAP-8, is an eight-amino-acid peptide sold as a topical way to soften expression lines. It is an extended version of [acetyl hexapeptide-8](/peptides/acetyl-hexapeptide-8) (Argireline) and is described as imitating part of SNAP-25, a nerve protein needed to trigger muscle contraction. The only human studies found tested it inside multi-ingredient microneedle patches, so its own effect cannot be separated out.[^1][^2] **Evidence is limited**, and a skin product is not expected to act like an injection of botulinum toxin.
glance: Expression lines around the eyes and forehead
Serums and creams; also in some microneedle patches
Lab claims and two small combination-patch studies

blocks.text: Muscles contract when a nerve ending releases acetylcholine. That release depends on a set of proteins called the SNARE complex, which includes SNAP-25. Botulinum toxin cuts SNAP-25, which is why injections relax muscles.

SNAP-8 is described as a copy of a stretch of SNAP-25 that competes for a place in the complex, so slightly less acetylcholine is released. This neurotransmitter-inhibiting approach is one of four peptide categories in a 2009 review of topical peptides (the others are signal, enzyme-inhibitor and carrier peptides).[^3] The mechanism is mainly shown in lab systems, and it is unclear how much peptide reaches nerve endings under the skin.

rows: 24 adults, eye-area patch vs placebo patch, 28 days
A microneedle patch with acetyl octapeptide-3, a vitamin C derivative and other ingredients improved eye wrinkles more than a hyaluronic acid-only patch; the peptide's share is unknown[^1]
Patches with acetyl octapeptide-3 plus other peptides and actives cut fine lines and wrinkles by 25.8% on instrumental analysis; the abstract describes no placebo arm[^2]
Related peptide: acetyl hexapeptide-8, 60 adults, 4 weeks
Randomized against placebo: 48.9% total efficacy versus 0% by clinical assessment, with lower skin roughness on replicas. This supports the idea for the shorter peptide, not SNAP-8 itself[^4]

blocks.text: Microneedle patches puncture the skin's outer layer, so they test delivery by a different route than an ordinary cream. For creams, size is a hurdle: molecules larger than about 500 daltons struggle to cross intact skin,[^5] and an eight-amino-acid peptide is more than twice that.

SNAP-8 appears in anti-wrinkle serums, eye creams and some microneedle patches. Creams are usually applied once or twice a day for several weeks before any change is judged. Ingredient lists rarely show how much is in a product.

The two patch studies reported good tolerance and no adverse effects, but they were small and short.[^1][^2] Because little peptide is expected to cross intact skin, effects on muscles elsewhere in the body are unlikely, though formal studies are lacking.
Cosmetics do not need FDA approval before sale, and a product that claims to change how the body works can be treated as a drug.[^6]

SNAP-8 is a plausible but unproven cosmetic peptide. Nothing found shows that it outperforms its shorter relative, and no study isolates its effect in people. If it appeals as part of a routine, expect subtle changes at most, and do not treat it as a substitute for medical treatments for deep lines.

evidence.label: Very limited: no stand-alone human trial found
evidence.text: Human data come only from small studies of combination patches, one with a placebo patch and one without a described control.[^1][^2] A systematic review of anti-aging cosmetic ingredients found good supporting data are often missing.[^7]

faq.a: It is sold as a longer, more potent version, but no head-to-head human trial was found. The best randomized evidence is for the shorter peptide, not SNAP-8.[^4]
No. Botulinum toxin is injected to cut SNAP-25 inside nerve endings and clearly relaxes muscles. A cream peptide would have to cross the skin first, and its effect, if any, is much smaller.

faq.q: Are microneedle patches with SNAP-8 better than creams?
faq.a: They deliver ingredients through tiny channels in the outer skin layer, and the small studies reported good tolerance.[^1][^2] Results cannot be credited to the peptide alone, and patches can still irritate skin.
